stages.reasoning: Introductions provide attitudes and possible future conflicts, but no crime, method, opportunity, or evidence yet. Vincent sounds somewhat more defensive because the inclusion of early work has already prompted expensive objections. Grant is implicated in catering instructions and donor relationships, while several guests signal money or provenance disputes. These are only narrative possibilities. I cannot identify a clear culprit or distinguish most characters meaningfully from these introductory remarks.

Artie now has an explicit employment motive: acceptance of the donor gift requires his resignation. Dada and Vincent face appropriation of creative credit, and Anne faces budget cuts. Security obscured camera access, while private service retained access and received the special toast glass. The historical poison bottle is potentially important, but its contents remain unverified and no murder has occurred in the released material. Motive and prospective opportunity remain spread across the cast.

The death follows the private toast, making service access and the engraved glass more relevant than generalized disputes. Artie benefits from preventing a gift that would remove him, although the notice emphasizes that none of those terms had been accepted. Brie has an occupational connection to the likely ingestion opportunity, but there is no direct evidence of contamination or even confirmed poisoning. The camera request may have facilitated concealment. I retain broad uncertainty pending statements and physical findings.

Everyone has an individualized conflict, making motive alone weak discrimination. Artie still faces the most direct personal loss, while Hugh concealed a false certificate and Elle diverted another client advance. Barb deliberately concealed the private camera feed, and Brie controlled a paid toast amid a disputed cheese charge. Several disputes concern correcting publicity rather than preventing ruin. Nothing yet ties any person to the bottle or glass at a specific moment. The plausible suspect field remains large.

Poisoning is confirmed and individualized: the shared punch and food were clean, while the glass and historical bottle contained active cyanide. The unattended glass between 6:32 and 7:04 presents a long contamination window, though service could also contaminate it afterward. The concealed split suggests deliberate handling of the bottle, directing attention toward collection staff and anyone with preview access. Barb has concealment opportunity and Brie glass access, but the facts still provide no unique timeline or witness link.

Elle combines preview attendance with a private-room visit beside the waiting glass, making her a stronger suspect. Brie brought culinary flavoring to that place and also controlled service, while Dada, Barb, Tess, and Mona acknowledge relevant visits or drink arrangements. The original-contents attachment undermines the innocuous caption and suggests knowledgeable preview attendees could recognize a poison source. Sue has a public-desk activity and Artie blocked the announcement. No suspect yet has a uniquely established source-to-glass chain.

The band scrap connects the bottle closure to the glass, although similarity without a torn-edge match is not unique proof. The open preview and bare glass remove physical access objections. Elle retains both stated contacts and a serious financial motive, while Brie retains direct glass access despite clean retained flavoring. Artie had already refused the gift and Tess would not automatically inherit the donor seat, weakening their motives. The unplugged camera eliminates technological footage assumptions but does not identify a poisoner.

Elle now falsely says the preview bottle was projected and the physical loan remained in the cupboard. Production retained only stitch slides, and the retained original preview frame shows the real bottle openly accessible. She earlier admitted preview attendance and placing fabric beside the unattended glass, joining source and target access. Her false physical-exclusion account directly obstructs the poisoning mechanism. Hugh and Penny also contradict documents, but their contradictions concern press contents and valuation rather than an established visit to the waiting glass.

accusation.reasoning: Elle attended the closed preview and admitted carrying her textile through the private room, rolling it beside the waiting glass while Grant was absent. The real bottle stood on an open support; the glass was bare, unattended, and later delivered with clean shared punch. Cyanide was found in the glass and bottle, and similar closure-band paper was in the glass. Her final assertion that the bottle was only a projection and the physical loan stayed in the cupboard conflicts with the original preview frame and the stitch-only production slides. This lie specifically erases her access to the poison source. Grant knew she had spent another client advance and used that vulnerability to demand pattern rights. Brie is the strongest alternative because she dosed the glass with flavoring, but the retained container was clean and her account agrees with the paid order. Hugh and Penny tell other demonstrable lies, yet neither has the same established source-and-glass route.
accusation.feedback: The people generally sound distinct under pressure. Artie counting chairs, Frank obsessing about a chair position, and Al asking to call home work especially well because their attention slips toward habits and actual responsibilities. Reed and Claire have an engaging strained relationship, and Brie and Barb protecting staff make them more than occupational suspects. The central poisoning route is solvable before voting: exposed source, unattended individual glass, clean communal supply, and an access-denying statement contradicted by independently retained images. I appreciate that the band scrap is explicitly similar stock rather than falsely treated as an exact forensic match. The event feels plausible locally, though the full cast creates a conspicuously assembled pattern: practically everyone has a concealed professional compromise, a donor conflict, and a precisely retained correction. Much of the final round sounds like testimony responding to a technical checklist. It remains emotionally effective, but the large number of parallel files dilutes momentum. I found no contradiction that defeats the core solution; the certainty comes from converging evidence and the consequential lie rather than exclusive physical access.

issues.detail: The final answers precisely resolve technical alternatives such as projection, camera installation, and stopper-band construction. Across the whole round, that coordinated completeness makes the scene resemble evidentiary testimony more than spontaneous dinner conversation.
issues.suggested_fix: Keep all decisive facts but move one or two technical clarifications into short witness notes, letting those speakers spend the saved lines responding to another person.

issues.detail: The large retained-paper release includes separate valuation, press-caption, delivery, and commission disputes alongside the poison chain. These useful secondary lies compete for attention at the last investigative checkpoint.
issues.suggested_fix: Visually group secondary financial corrections in one compact document, retaining their explicit contradictions and avoiding additional explanatory speeches.

finale.feedback: The confession follows the pre-vote route closely: the physical bottle, stitch-only slides, and unattended glass already exposed the projection claim as a meaningful lie. Taking poison at the preview and using it later supplies the admitted action rather than a newly necessary clue. The explanation that repayment could not erase exposure fits the earlier client-advance account and sharpens the motive without rescuing an otherwise unsolvable case. The last line about never touching the fabric again is emotionally effective. The opening is somewhat forensic, reciting image evidence directly, but the personal ending earns its place. Hugh and Chip acknowledge bounded wrongdoing convincingly; their corrections preserve the distinction between concealment and murder.
